content: 1. The study published in JAMA in 2020 (volume 323, pages 863-884) provides a comprehensive analysis of low back pain, focusing on its diagnosis and treatment strategies. 2. Koes BW, van Tulder MW, and Thomas S, in their 2006 BMJ article (volume 332, pages 1430-1434), discuss the clinical approaches to diagnosing and managing low back pain, emphasizing evidence-based practices. 3. Henschke N et al., in their 2009 Arthritis Rheum study (volume 60, pages 3072-3080), investigate the prevalence of serious spinal pathologies in patients presenting with acute low back pain in primary care settings, highlighting the importance of screening. 4. Hill JC et al., in their 2011 Spine article (volume 36, pages 2168-2175), examine clinical outcomes in primary care patients with low back pain and referred leg pain, providing insights into prognosis and management. 5. Williamson E et al., in their 2021 Spine study (volume 46, pages 54-61), explore the prevalence of back and leg pain in older adults in England and its association with adverse health outcomes, using a cross-sectional approach. 6. Kongsted A et al., in their 2012 BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders article (volume 13, article 236), compare patients with low back pain alone to those with additional leg pain or nerve root involvement, offering a detailed cross-sectional analysis. 7. Muthuri SG et al., in their 2018 Pain study (volume 159, pages 764-774), analyze longitudinal profiles of back pain across adulthood and their relationship with childhood factors, using data from the 1946 British birth cohort. 8. Da Silva T et al., in their 2017 systematic review in J Orthop Sports Phys Ther (volume 47, pages 305-313), assess the risk of recurrence in low back pain, synthesizing evidence from multiple studies. 9. Da Silva T et al., in their 2019 J Physiother article (volume 65, pages 159-165), report that recurrence of low back pain is common, based on findings from a prospective inception cohort study. 10. Kyronlahti SM et al., in their 2021 Eur J Public Health study (volume 32, pages 497-503), investigate trajectories of low back pain from midlife to retirement and its impact on functional ability in old age. 11. Chou R and Shekelle P, in their 2010 JAMA article (volume 303, pages 1295-1302), discuss predictive factors for persistent disabling low back pain, providing a framework for early identification and intervention. 12. Itz CJ et al., in their 2013 systematic review in Eur J Pain (volume 17, pages 5-15), analyze the clinical course of non-specific low back pain in primary care, emphasizing variability in patient outcomes. 13. Kongsted A et al., in their 2016 BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders article (volume 17, article 220), summarize key findings from a decade of trajectory research in low back pain, identifying patterns and predictors of chronicity. 14. Parreira PCS et al., in their 2017 Pain study (volume 158, pages 1571-1576), conduct a longitudinal analysis of the influence of comorbidities and lifestyle factors on low back pain in older men. 15. Gaskin DJ and Richard P, in their 2012 J Pain article (volume 13, pages 715-724), estimate the economic costs of pain in the United States, with a focus on the burden of low back pain. 16. Jackson T et al., in their 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis in Anesth Analg (volume 123, pages 739-748), evaluate the global burden of chronic pain without clear etiology in lowand middle-income countries, proposing new assessment methods. 17. Dagenais S et al., in their 2008 Spine J article (volume 8, pages 8-20), systematically review the cost of illness studies for low back pain in the United States and internationally, highlighting economic implications. 18. Schofield DJ et al., in their 2012 Spine study (volume 37, pages 1156-1163), examine the impact of back problems on labor force participation and income poverty in Australia. 19. Schofield D et al., in their 2012 Pain article (volume 153, pages 203-210), analyze the effect of back problems on retirement wealth, emphasizing the financial burden of chronic conditions. 20. Lacey RJ et al., in their 2013 Eur J Public Health study (volume 23, pages 534-540), investigate the influence of life course socioeconomic position on chronic disabling pain in older adults. 21. Sharma S et al., in their 2019 J Glob Health article (volume 9, article 010304), discuss the challenges of delivering appropriate care for low back pain in lowand middle-income countries, using Nepal as a case study. 22. Shmagel A et al., in their 2016 Arthritis Care Res study (volume 68, pages 1688-1694), provide epidemiological data on chronic low back pain in U.S. adults, based on the 2009-2010 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. 23. Ikeda T et al., in their 2019 Int J Equity Health article (volume 18, article 15), explore socioeconomic inequalities in low back pain among older adults in Japan, using data from the JAGES cross-sectional study. 24. Karran EL et al., in their 2020 Pain systematic review (volume 161, pages 2476-2493), examine the social determinants of health in relation to low back pain, synthesizing evidence on disparities and outcomes. 25. WHO guidelines for the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults emphasize evidence-based approaches in primary and community care settings. 26. Beyera GK et al., in their 2019 systematic review in Rheumatol Int (volume 39, pages 1663-1679), analyze healthcare utilization patterns for low back pain, based on population-based observational studies. 27. Deyo RA et al., in their 2009 J Am Board Fam Med article (volume 22, pages 62-68), critique the overtreatment of chronic back pain, advocating for more conservative management strategies. 28. Wong AY et al., in their 2017 Scoliosis Spinal Disord article (volume 12, article 14), review risk factors, management options, and future directions for low back pain in older adults. 29. Vigdal ØN et al., in their 2021 BMJ Open article (volume 11, article e053229), analyze characteristics of older adults with back pain and their choice of primary care providers, using data from the BACE-N cohort study. 30. Dionne CE et al., in their 2006 systematic review in Age Ageing (volume 35, pages 229-234), question whether back pain prevalence truly decreases with age, synthesizing evidence from multiple studies.
